The two models behind the lists, and what each is for
F1 lens → the action list: who to approach. A model trained on real F1 sponsors and scored forward in time (learned on the past, tested on a later period). This is the shipped ranking.
Cross-sport lens → a wider discovery view: who sponsors sport at all. A second model, useful for surfacing names the action list cannot see.
Two lists, two models. The charts below show what drove each ranking, the strongest predictors of signing. (A third model, the RQ2 hazard, drives the worklist on the “Closing the deal” tab.)

What makes a company rank highly

Driven by whether a company recently paid for sponsorship elsewhere, then whether it is big enough to pay again (headcount, revenue), then the size of its previous deals.

Driven mostly by sheer commercial size and global reach: revenue, headcount, and how many countries and F1 markets it operates in. Prior sponsorship barely features here, because across all sports most big spenders have already sponsored something, so it stops telling likely signers apart.

Choose a lens
# Rank: how strongly this company matches past F1 sponsors Capacity: why they can afford it, revenue and headcount from our Salesforce records News trigger Why now: leadership changes, expansion, M&A and IPOs, advertising and rebrands, fundraising. Display only, never in the score.
What ranks a company. How recently a company last sponsored anything is the strongest signal, ahead of size and revenue. Headcount, revenue and the value of past deals come next. No news text, snippet or model output enters any score. News counts enter two models: they contribute to the cross-sport discovery score, and in the open-deal ranking model two are coverability controls, whether we see news for an account at all and how much, with the trigger term tested against them, which came back a tie. The F1 action list has no news feature of any kind, so here news is a why-now prompt on a company already ranked, not a ranking input.
Select a company from the list to see its dossier.
Two lists, two questions. The F1 list asks who looks like a Formula 1 sponsor. This wider list asks who sponsors sport at all. They disagree on purpose: a regional business that backs local teams can top this list and sit far down the F1 one. That gap is measured. This wider model ranks real F1 signers no better than chance, which is why the F1 list is the action list and this one is for discovery.

Ranked by the deployed cross-sport model, covers the 3,500 accounts it scores (the prospects it can size); every other company remains in the F1 lens and search. Discovery only, not an action list.

Showing the full model order. 35 of 60 are sized from Salesforce revenue, marked with a dot.
Select a company from the list to see its dossier.
How to read a fallback rank. Filed accounts are not available for 35 of these 60 companies, so their revenue rank is positioned against the companies that do carry a Salesforce revenue figure, a smaller and differently distributed group than the filed-accounts one. Ranks built that way are not directly comparable with the rest of the list and tend to sit too high. Every other driver shown on these cards is observed, not estimated. Treat the ordering of fallback-ranked companies as indicative and read the drivers rather than the position.
How to read it

A ranked starting point, not an automatic decision. The F1 model is genuinely more accurate at spotting F1 sponsors than a general one, but the effect is modest, so treat the list as a well-evidenced prompt for the team's judgement.

Evaluating Proposal

What drives the odds, and what the model is

What separates a deal that closes. We tested every engagement factor we could measure against whether the deal signed. Three came through, and all three describe what the deal already was when it arrived: the client had been to a Grand Prix, it came through an agency we already work with, or it was a renewal. Everything a rep does to a deal came back a tie. Use this to choose which open deals get your week.

What the open-deal model found
What works.Grand Prix hospitality, a warm agency channel, and renewals. All three are things about the deal, not things you do to it.
What does not.Emailing more often, adding hospitality invitations, and press coverage before or during talks. Each was tested and came back a tie.
What that means.The list ranks which deals are worth your time. It does not tell you what to do to a deal, because nothing we could measure a rep doing changed the odds.

Every factor we tested against closing. The deployed model scores on five of these, marked ◆; the proposal arms were tested and are shown here for completeness, not used to rank.◆ in the deployed model

No proposal, no win. Of 310 opportunities that never had a proposal of any kind, not one closed. That is the only hard rule in this analysis.

Engagement archetypes

Does how you work a deal change whether it closes? No. Of 210 closed deals that got as far as a proposal, the shape with the most logged activity closed least often at 22%, and the shape that reached a senior decision-maker closed most at 58%. That gap disappears once you account for who owned the deal, and only two of these five shapes have enough deals to trust at all. Working a weak deal harder is not a lever. Shares are of those 210, of which 42% closed won.
ArchetypeShareReached proposal, then closed wonCharacter
Email-heavy, high-touch2%75% (n=4, too few to trust)every channel firing at once, a handful of extreme-touch outliers (read cautiously)
GP-attended6%69% (n=13, too few to trust)hosted at a Grand Prix (legacy proposal-anchor snapshot; the corrected GP-attendance source finds many more attendances, see the forest below)
Senior-engaged12%58% (n=26)reached a senior decision-maker early
Average / mixed engagement71%38% (n=150)the base-rate majority, ordinary, mixed engagement
Activity-logged, high-touch9%22% (n=18, too few to trust)lots of logged activity, little traction

Why the results read the way they do: shape does not predict which deal closes once you control for who owns it, so we do not tag live opportunities with an archetype. What predicts closure is the hazard model in the drivers figure above.

Why the counts here differ from the table above. Above: 210 whole deals, already closed, that reached a proposal at any point, asking did it sign. Here: stage-to-stage moves logged in Salesforce since 2024, asking did it move to the next stage. Different unit, different question. The two figures near 42% are a coincidence and mean different things.

What moves a deal to the next stage

Where deals actually stop. Read the 2024-onward column. Salesforce only began tracking stage history then, so the pooled and pre-2024 rates are floors, not real drops. On that basis 37% of deals leave Discovery and 47% leave Opportunity Qualified, and those two ranges overlap, so we cannot say a deal’s odds improve once it is qualified. Progression then falls to 26% in Development, and that fall is real because the ranges do not overlap. Development is where a qualified deal goes quiet, so a deal sitting there is the one to chase or close out this week. Stages beyond Development have ranges too wide to separate; read those as not enough data yet.Built is how many opportunities entered a stage; supervised is those whose next step we can actually see (an open deal still sitting in a stage is not counted); advanced is those that then moved to a later stage.

The 2024 onward column counts only opportunities that closed in 2024 or later, when Salesforce began recording stage history. That is the column to read.

                                              • Grand Prix hospitality: higher closing odds at the opportunity level in every specification, but the size is not identified at 38 events (the hazard ratio swings from about 1.2× to 13× with an untuned penalty; the deployed point estimate is 3.1×, and it ties under fuller controls). A prioritisation proxy, not a lever a rep can pull; from the corrected GP-attendance source.
                                              • Warm channel, agency 2.0× [1.4, 3.0], renewal 1.9× [1.4, 2.5] (per standard deviation). These are prioritisation modifiers that proxy account quality, not rep levers: routing a cold deal through an agency does not make it an agency deal. They tell you which open deals deserve your hours, not what to do to a deal.
                                              • News during engagement, a clean null, and defended on coverage rather than waved away: wins had news 43% of the time, losses 36%, so the null is not an artefact of never observing news on the winners.
                                              • Cadence / momentum, a null. It is listed as a next-best action for prioritisation only. An earlier version of this page called it the "biggest modelled lift to closure"; it is a null arm, and that wording is withdrawn.
                                              • Grand Prix during Development, now testable but underpowered. The corrected source gives 3 wins across 52 exposed periods, too few to resolve a coefficient either way; on the old source there was no exposure at all, so it could not be tested. Too few to tell is not the same as no effect.
                                              What the model found, honestly

                                              Across the fitted cohort (930 opportunities and 38 wins in the person-period timing engine; 930/38 in the opportunity-level model), most logged engagement does not predict closure once rep identity and logging maturity are controlled, and rep identity remains the dominant signal, which is a finding about the data, not a lever. The hazard model's survivors are the warm-agency and renewal channels; Grand Prix hospitality survives at the opportunity level but ties under fuller controls, and all three prioritise rather than being levers a rep can pull. One further signal, average days between emails, is excluded as a logging-presence artefact: it is recorded on 690 stretches holding just 2 wins, which is too thin to fit, so what a model finds in it is which deals had email data at all. So the worklist leads with what survives, every "why now" is a real dated fact, and the nulls are reported as nulls.
